newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler sours on "shareholder value" image.
newsitem.headline: Daimler sours on "shareholder value" image.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG is wiping the expression "shareholder value" from its corporate vocabulary less than a year after spearheading its use in Germany and making the term a cornerstone of the group's strategy.

In an interview with a leading German business magazine, Daimler chairman Juergen Schrempp said the industrial giant would no longer utter anything about "shareholder value" here, saying the phrase had tarnished the company's image.
"In Germany I will not use this English term," Schrempp told WirtschaftsWoche magazine. "It has been reduced to an ideological battle cry."
A Daimler spokesman confirmed that the magazine had accurately reported Schrempp's remarks.
Schrempp's abandonment of at least the terminology of shareholder value comes just as the government is trying to promote both the phrase and the concept with the privatisation of Deutsche Telekom.
It also raises deeper questions about Daimler and how it weighs pursuit of profits against protecting jobs and living standards for its employees, that are the envy of the most industrial nations.

Schrempp claims dropping shareholder value from the company vocabulary does not mean that the company is any less devoted to making money, only that unions will no longer be able to use it against the company.

German unions, who have held wildcat strikes against Mercedes-Benz recently, have derided Daimler's efforts to improve shareholder value, saying the company should not sacrifice labour at the altar of profits.

Instead of shareholder value, Daimler will in the future use a German term which means "the need of improving the value of the company" (Notwendigkeit der Unternehmenswertsteigerung) -- a phrasing clearly more difficult to fit on a union banner.
"I am only giving up a term with negative connotations without of course giving up on the concept," Schrempp said.
But the decision may be one of more than just semantics.
The German press has carried several stories in recent days saying Schrempp, who has developed a "Rambo" image for his ruthless cost-cutting, now wants a kinder, gentler image.

Schrempp first earned a "tough-guy" status for his decision to cut off funds to struggling aircraft unit Fokker and has since been criticised for his plans to reorganise Daimler, bringing individual units closer into the group structure.
But in recent comments, Schrempp has shown signs of a re-think in his tough approach to union demands and has spoken more often of reaching a consensus on labour issues.
The German media has even noted that Schrempp's decision to abandon his once trademark angular-shaped glasses in favour of rounded tortoise-shell spectacles shows he is striving for a make over.
Although carefully guarding his words, Schrempp's comments indicated he would take a full range of issues into account when plotting the group's future.

The chairman, who in the past has called shareholders the top priority, said the company will have to consider what it calls "the magic triangle" in making strategic decisions -- considering its customers, shareholders and the workforce.
Shareholders, he said, constituted only one part of this triangle, even if they do deserve a little special attention.
"When a company like Daimler-Benz has neglected its shareholders for six years, it is my duty to rebalance the triangle," he said.
